basic_info.name: Vladan Joler
basic_info.active_years: 2010-present (SHARE Foundation founded 2012; artistic practice and academic work from earlier)

practice_description.medium: Large-scale relational diagrams, counter-cartography, data visualization, investigative research-as-art, video animation
practice_description.practice_summary: Vladan Joler creates monumental diagrammatic maps that render visible the hidden infrastructures of AI, digital labor, resource extraction, and surveillance capitalism. His practice blends investigative journalism, data mining, critical cartography, and philosophical inquiry into artworks that function simultaneously as research outputs, educational tools, and aesthetic objects.
practice_description.methodology: Joler combines methodologies from investigative journalism, data mining, network topology analysis, and critical cartography. He assembles 'concept maps' from statistical research, data mining, philosophy (ancient and contemporary), media theory, fiction, sociology, and economics. The resulting diagrams are composed of lines, arrows, symbols, process diagrams, and descriptions entangled in large networks. He works through SHARE Lab (a research and investigation lab he founded) and collaborates with researchers like Kate Crawford (Anatomy of an AI System) and Matteo Pasquinelli (Nooscope). His maps are built through extensive investigative research that can span years, then rendered as large-scale black-and-white diagrammatic prints, websites, manuals, and video animations. He explicitly leverages the artist's freedom to combine methodologies that would be siloed in academic or journalistic contexts.

relevance_to_sense_room.relevance_summary: Joler's work is the most direct precedent for A(DAI)'s concept of graph-as-exhibition. His large-scale relational diagrams ARE artworks where the graph structure — nodes, edges, relationships — is the primary aesthetic and intellectual material. New Extractivism demonstrates that a network diagram can function as a major exhibition-scale artwork.
relevance_to_sense_room.art_as_substrate: Yes, in a distinctive way. Joler's diagrams are substrate-like in that they provide a ground layer of interconnected knowledge that viewers navigate and explore. The diagram functions as a landscape or territory rather than a discrete object. However, they are static substrates (fixed prints/websites) rather than generative ones.
relevance_to_sense_room.relational_composition: Yes — this is the core of the practice. Every Joler work is fundamentally a relational composition: concepts, institutions, processes, materials, and actors are positioned as nodes connected by explicit relationships (arrows, lines, flows). The artwork IS the graph. The meaning emerges from the connections between elements rather than from any single element. New Extractivism's 33 chapters are linked through a complex web of conceptual relationships.
relevance_to_sense_room.self_recomposing: No. Joler's works are fixed compositions — carefully researched and authored diagrams that do not change once completed. They are static maps of dynamic systems. The systems they depict are self-recomposing, but the artworks themselves are not.

works.title: New Extractivism
works.description: A cartographic project comprising a large-scale map, a manual, and a video animation that guides viewers through the 'traps, tunnels, and slippery corridors' of world-scale extractive infrastructure. Organized in 33 chapters exploring power, control, digital labor, colonialism, and exploitation of nature. Exhibited internationally including at Aksioma, Ars Electronica, and Warsaw Biennale.
works.relevance: The most direct precedent for graph-as-exhibition in A(DAI). Demonstrates that a relational diagram can function as a major artwork — the map IS the exhibition. The 33-chapter structure shows how graph-organized knowledge can be navigated as aesthetic experience. Available at extractivism.online as a web-native work.

works.title: Anatomy of an AI System
works.description: Collaboration with Kate Crawford (AI Now Institute, NYU). A large-scale map and long-form essay investigating the human labor, data, and planetary resources required to build and operate an Amazon Echo. Visualizes three extractive processes: material resources, human labor, and data. Won 2019 Design of the Year Award (Design Museum London), S+T+ARTS Prize Honorary Mention. In permanent collections of MoMA, V&A, Design Museum, Ars Electronica Center.
works.relevance: Demonstrates how a single relational diagram can achieve major institutional recognition as artwork. The exploded-view methodology — tracing a consumer object back through its entire supply chain of materials, labor, and data — is a model for how A(DAI) could trace art-world phenomena through their full relational context.

works.title: Invisible Infrastructures (SHARE Lab)
works.description: A series of data investigations using network topology, data mining, and data visualization to create atlases of internet architecture, social media power structures, and algorithmic transparency. The first investigation mapped the physical infrastructure of the internet.
works.relevance: Establishes the methodology of infrastructure-mapping-as-art. SHARE Lab's investigative approach — combining technical analysis with critical visualization — is a model for how A(DAI) could investigate and visualize the digital arts field's own infrastructure.

protocol_art_resonance.protocol_art_summary: Joler does not design protocols or systems as artwork; rather, he maps and critically analyzes existing protocols, systems, and infrastructures AS artwork. His practice is diagnostic rather than constructive — revealing the hidden architectures of power rather than building alternative ones. However, the SHARE Foundation (which he founded) does build civic tech infrastructure, creating a link between his artistic mapping practice and actual infrastructure construction.
protocol_art_resonance.system_designed: SHARE Foundation — a civic tech and digital rights organization based in Novi Sad, Serbia. SHARE Lab — a research and investigation lab for algorithmic transparency and invisible infrastructures. Knowing Machines — a collaborative research project developing critical methodologies and tools for understanding ML training datasets. These are research and advocacy infrastructures rather than artistic protocols per se.

commons_orientation.commons_summary: Strongly commons-oriented. Works are published under Creative Commons licenses (CC BY-NC-SA 4.0 for some works, CC BY 4.0 for others). New Extractivism is freely accessible at extractivism.online. Anatomy of an AI System is freely available at anatomyof.ai. SHARE Foundation is a nonprofit dedicated to digital rights and open internet. The practice is fundamentally about making invisible systems visible to the public — a knowledge-commons project. Joler's academic position at the University of Novi Sad reinforces the public-knowledge orientation.

governance_model.governance_detail: Joler works as a solo artist for his diagrammatic works but within collaborative structures: SHARE Lab is a research collective, SHARE Foundation is a nonprofit with institutional governance, and major works involve co-authorship (Kate Crawford for Anatomy of an AI, Matteo Pasquinelli for Nooscope). His academic position at the Academy of Arts, University of Novi Sad, adds an institutional governance layer. The practice blends solo artistic vision with collaborative research and institutional structures.

consent_and_authorship.consent_approach: Joler's work is investigative — it maps systems and structures using publicly accessible information, data mining, and research. No personal data from individuals is used as primary material. The work investigates institutions and systems rather than individuals, though it names key figures in power structures. Consent is not a primary concern because the material is structural/systemic rather than personal.
consent_and_authorship.authorship_model: Collaborative authorship for major works (Crawford + Joler for Anatomy, Pasquinelli + Joler for Nooscope). Solo authorship for works like New Extractivism. SHARE Lab works are collectively authored. The practice acknowledges collaboration explicitly through co-authorship credit. Creative Commons licensing further distributes authorial control by allowing reuse and adaptation.

liveness_and_duration.temporal_detail: Works are fixed compositions — diagrams, prints, websites, and videos that do not change once published. They are research outputs frozen at their moment of completion. However, the web-based versions (extractivism.online, anatomyof.ai) remain accessible indefinitely as living reference documents. New Extractivism includes a video animation that unfolds the diagram over time, adding a temporal dimension to the viewing experience.

data_materiality.data_sources: Statistical research and data mining from public sources, corporate filings, academic publications, philosophical texts (ancient and contemporary), media theory, fiction, sociology, economics, network topology analysis, supply chain documentation, environmental impact reports. The 'data' is research itself — assembled from diverse publicly available sources through investigative methods.
data_materiality.data_provenance: Publicly available information, academic research, institutional publications, open data. No scraped personal data. The investigative methodology relies on publicly accessible technology and information. Creative Commons licensing of the outputs reinforces the public-domain orientation of the source material.

embedding_space_relevance.embedding_summary: Joler does not work with computational embedding spaces or latent spaces. His 'embedding' is conceptual — positioning ideas, institutions, and processes within a hand-crafted relational space (the diagram). The spatial arrangement of elements in his maps is determined by research and editorial judgment rather than algorithmic computation. However, his maps could be understood as manual, human-authored analogs to what embedding spaces do computationally: positioning entities in relation to each other based on their connections.
embedding_space_relevance.multimodal: Works span visual (diagrams, prints), textual (essays, manuals), and video (animations) modalities but these are not unified through a computational embedding space. They are complementary presentations of the same research.

exhibition_modality.spatial_description: Works manifest as: (1) large-scale prints displayed on gallery walls — monumental black-and-white diagrams that viewers navigate physically by moving along the surface, (2) websites that allow zooming and scrolling navigation of the diagram digitally, (3) printed manuals/books, (4) video animations that unfold the diagram over time. The physical exhibition experience involves standing before wall-scale diagrams and tracing connections — the viewer's eye movement through the diagram replicates graph traversal.

interoperability.composability: High conceptual composability. The Creative Commons licensing means works can be reused, adapted, and built upon. The diagrammatic format is inherently composable — elements and connections from one diagram could be integrated into larger knowledge networks. The web-based versions are linkable and embeddable. However, there are no APIs, standard data formats, or machine-readable graph structures exported from the works [uncertain].
interoperability.technical_openness: Open. Works are published under Creative Commons licenses, freely accessible on the web, and designed for public knowledge dissemination. The research methodologies are documented and shared. Source data and references are cited.

technical_approach.stack: Data mining and network topology analysis tools, data visualization software, vector graphics tools for diagram creation, web development for online versions (extractivism.online, anatomyof.ai), video animation for temporal unfoldings of diagrams. The emphasis is on research methodology and visual communication rather than computational complexity. Specific software tools are not prominently disclosed [uncertain].

network_position.scene_affiliation: Critical art/technology, tactical media, investigative art, design and information visualization, digital rights advocacy, academic research (AI ethics, critical data studies). Bridges art world (MoMA, V&A collections, Ars Electronica), academic research (AI Now Institute, University of Novi Sad), civic society (SHARE Foundation, digital rights), and design (Design Museum awards). Connected to the broader critical AI/technology community including Kate Crawford, Trevor Paglen, Matteo Pasquinelli, Knowing Machines project.
network_position.connections: Refik Anadol (both engage with AI as artistic subject but from opposing positions — Joler critically maps AI's extractive infrastructure while Anadol celebrates its generative aesthetic potential; Anatomy of an AI System is implicitly a critical counterpoint to celebratory AI art). Suzanne Treister (shared practice of knowledge-network mapping as art, though Joler focuses on technological infrastructure while Treister maps historical/political/occult knowledge networks; both use the diagram as primary artistic form).

potential_role_in_adai.role_detail: Joler's work is the most direct precedent for A(DAI)'s graph-as-exhibition concept. New Extractivism and Anatomy of an AI System demonstrate that relational diagrams can function as major artworks — the graph IS the art. His commons orientation (Creative Commons licensing, free web access, nonprofit infrastructure through SHARE Foundation) aligns strongly with A(DAI)'s commons-first values. His critical mapping methodology could be applied to mapping the digital arts field itself. Potential roles: (1) artwork within A(DAI)'s graph that maps the infrastructure of the field, (2) methodological reference for how A(DAI) visualizes its own intelligence graph, (3) critical friend who can identify extractive patterns within A(DAI)'s own infrastructure. His Novi Sad/Serbia base also connects to European digital arts networks.
